profile.title: Outpatient Nutrition Assessment in a Precontemplative Patient with Chronic Pain, Obesity, and Hidden Caregiver Burden
profile.summary: This case trains dietetics students to conduct a telehealth nutrition assessment with a blunt, precontemplative patient whose chronic pain, obesity, and hyperlipidemia are compounded by a hidden caregiving burden for her elderly mother. It emphasizes rapport-building with a guarded patient, recognizing a self-report-versus-record mismatch (multivitamin refill history and reported water intake versus actual soda-heavy fluid pattern) without confrontation, screening for opioid-related GI effects on intake, and delivering stage-appropriate motivational interviewing focused on small, low-effort dietary swaps rather than demanding major lifestyle change.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Perth Amboy, NJ, sitting in a cluttered kitchen/living area

patient.name: Jayme Littel
patient.occupation: Former retail stock associate, currently unemployed
patient.appearance: Sits stiffly on a kitchen chair, shifting her weight and wincing slightly when she turns to reach for her phone; mild facial puffiness; limited neck range of motion visible when she turns to look off-camera; flat affect, minimal eye contact at first, arms often crossed; a small succulent and a worn paperback visible on the counter behind her

persona.personality: Blunt, impatient, wants to get to the point; doesn't do small talk; comes across as tired and guarded more than hostile, with a dry sense of humor that surfaces once she warms up slightly
persona.communicationStyle: Gives short, flat, clipped answers initially; needs a question rephrased and asked a second, gentler way before she opens up further; dislikes being lectured or having her weight brought up without a clear reason tied to her actual pain or energy
persona.emotionalState: Tired, guarded, mildly defensive about her eating habits and weight; softens somewhat if she feels heard rather than judged; underlying stress about caregiving and finances she doesn't volunteer easily
persona.background: Jayme is a former retail stock associate from Perth Amboy, NJ, currently unemployed. She's married, and grew up in a working-class household where meals were whatever was fastest between shifts—nobody taught her to cook and she never saw the point of learning. She keeps a small succulent on her windowsill ('the one thing I haven't killed') and rereads a worn paperback when back pain keeps her up at night. She used to enjoy walking her dog before her back got bad, now a neighbor helps out with that. Food, to her, has always been fuel, not a ritual, and she doesn't attach much meaning to it beyond getting through the day.
speechExamples: I eat whatever's fast, that's about it.
I don't see what any of this has to do with my back.
Fine, if you really want to know...
Nobody ever explains why any of this actually matters.
I'm not going to start meal-prepping, if that's what you're getting at.
concerns: Worried about keeping up with rent given her unemployment
Annoyed that every doctor visit turns into a conversation about her weight
Doesn't want vague 'eat healthy' advice without a clear explanation of why it matters for her pain or energy

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition assessment with Jayme Littel, a 35-year-old woman referred for obesity and high cholesterol in the context of chronic pain management. This is a new nutrition assessment visit. Review the available chart information before the call, then conduct your assessment and counseling via video.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Referred for nutrition assessment related to obesity, high cholesterol, and chronic pain management
scenario.openingLine: Yeah, hi. I guess my doctor wanted me to talk to someone about my eating. I don't really know what there is to say — I eat whatever's fast, that's about it.
tasks: Take a focused diet history, including a 24-hour recall and usual meal pattern
Review relevant anthropometrics and laboratory results and relate them to her nutrition status
Identify barriers to improving her dietary intake, including any time, financial, or caregiving-related constraints
Screen for medication-related factors (such as GI side effects) that may be affecting her appetite or intake
Deliver patient-centered nutrition education and counseling using motivational interviewing appropriate to her stage of readiness to change
Document your findings and plan using the ADIME format

actions.name: Visual inspection via video (posture, facial appearance, affect)
actions.result: Patient sits stiffly, shifts weight and winces when reaching; mild facial puffiness noted; limited neck range of motion when turning; flat affect with minimal eye contact initially.

actions.name: 24-hour diet recall
actions.result: Morning: black coffee, no breakfast. Midday: often skipped or a bag of chips/candy bar from a convenience store. Evening: frozen lasagna or fast-food chicken nuggets and fries. Beverages: 3-4 diet sodas across the day, minimal plain water. No fruits or vegetables reported in the recall.

actions.name: Usual meal pattern and timing assessment
actions.result: Irregular pattern: coffee in the morning, lunch frequently skipped, larger convenience-food dinner later in the evening once 'things calm down.'

actions.name: Fluid/beverage intake assessment
actions.result: Patient reports drinking 'a lot of water' when asked directly, but diet history obtained in the same visit lists several diet sodas and coffee daily with minimal plain water intake described.

actions.name: GI symptom and appetite screening (nausea, constipation, appetite changes)
actions.result: Patient reports occasional nausea and constipation she attributes to her pain medication, affecting how much she eats on some days; states she has not raised this with other providers.

actions.name: Physical activity assessment
actions.result: Minimal activity reported; pain limits standing or walking for extended periods; mostly sedentary at home.

actions.name: Review pharmacy refill history
actions.result: Multivitamin: single fill recorded over a year ago, no refills since. Fentanyl patches and Percocet show refills consistent with prescribed regimen.

actions.name: Supplement and OTC use assessment
actions.result: Patient reports taking her multivitamin 'most days.' Occasional ibuprofen for sinus headaches on top of prescribed pain medication. Saline nasal spray used for congestion.

actions.name: Sodium/convenience food pattern assessment
actions.result: Diet dominated by frozen entrees, fast food, and salty snack foods; patient has not reviewed nutrition labels and is unaware of sodium content of her usual choices.

artifacts.body: 35 y/o F with obesity (BMI 31.5), hyperlipidemia (LDL 208.8, total cholesterol 290), chronic low back and neck pain, and chronic sinusitis, managed on fentanyl patch and Percocet for pain. Referring to dietetics for nutrition assessment and counseling given elevated lipids and BMI 30+. Patient has expressed limited interest in dietary change at prior visits; recommend motivational interviewing approach.

objectives.text: Build rapport with a blunt, guarded patient using open-ended, non-judgmental questioning, allowing reluctant information such as caregiving burden to surface only with repeated, gentler inquiry
Assess nutrition-relevant anthropometrics and laboratory data and relate elevated BMI and lipid panel findings to the patient's dietary pattern and overall nutrition status
Identify time, financial, and caregiving-related barriers to improving dietary intake, including the hidden burden of caring for an elderly family member
Screen for medication-related gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, constipation) that may be affecting appetite and oral intake, and recognize when these have not previously been reported

Reconcile patient self-report of supplement and fluid habits with diet history and pharmacy records, exploring discrepancies using motivational interviewing techniques appropriate to a precontemplative stage of change
Deliver patient-centered nutrition education on practical, low-effort dietary swaps within her convenience-food pattern, avoiding a weight-focused frame given her frustration with prior visits

answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive sodium/convenience-food and sugar-sweetened beverage intake related to caregiving time burden and low nutrition-related health literacy, as evidenced by elevated LDL/total cholesterol and BMI 31.5 kg/m2 (nutrition diagnosis: PES statement — Excessive sodium and simple carbohydrate/sugar-sweetened beverage intake related to limited time/energy from caregiving responsibilities and low nutrition-related health literacy as evidenced by reliance on frozen/fast food, several diet sodas daily, minimal fruit/vegetable intake, and labs showing total cholesterol 290 mg/dL and LDL 208.8 mg/dL)
differential: Primary nutrition diagnosis: inconsistent/undesirable food choices related to caregiving burden and low health literacy
Inadequate fluid intake (water) related to habitual reliance on diet soda/coffee
Altered GI function (nausea/constipation) related to opioid therapy affecting oral intake pattern
Self-monitoring mismatch: reported supplement/fluid adherence vs. actual pattern (not a true clinical differential, but a documentation discrepancy to explore)
keyFindings: BMI 31.5 kg/m2 (weight 86.7 kg, height 165.8 cm) consistent with obesity
Total cholesterol 290 mg/dL and LDL 208.8 mg/dL, both above reference range; HDL and triglycerides within normal limits
Irregular meal pattern: coffee only in morning, frequently skips lunch, large convenience dinner at night
Diet dominated by frozen entrees, fast food, and gas-station snacks; minimal fruits/vegetables
Several diet sodas daily and minimal plain water intake, despite patient reporting she drinks 'a lot of water'
Pharmacy refill record shows multivitamin purchased once over a year ago with no refills, despite patient reporting she takes it 'most days'
Reports nausea and constipation she attributes to pain medication, which has not been discussed with prior providers and may be reducing/altering her intake
Chronic pain limits standing/cooking/shopping; caregiving duties for her mother consume most of her day, leaving little time for her own meals or rest
Precontemplative stage of change; does not believe diet is related to her pain symptoms
plan: Complete ADIME note documenting 24-hour recall, usual intake pattern, and barriers identified
Nutrition diagnosis (PES) focused on excessive convenience/sodium/sugar-sweetened beverage intake related to caregiving time burden and low health literacy, evidenced by labs and BMI
Use motivational interviewing: reflective listening, avoid direct confrontation about the multivitamin/water discrepancy, explore ambivalence about change
Offer plain-language, concrete education linking sodium/saturated fat intake to cholesterol numbers without over-emphasizing weight

Suggest small, low-effort swaps within her existing convenience-food pattern (e.g., lower-sodium frozen meal options, pairing a quick fruit/vegetable with meals, swapping one diet soda for flavored water) rather than meal-prep demands

Screen for and acknowledge opioid-related GI symptoms (nausea, constipation) and their effect on appetite/intake; recommend she discuss with prescribing provider and consider fiber/fluid strategies as tolerated
Address hydration pattern gently, normalizing that habits took time to build and swaps can be gradual
Acknowledge caregiving burden as a barrier without requiring her to disclose further; validate without probing into medication-sharing specifics
Arrange follow-up visit to reassess readiness to change and reinforce rapport before pushing further goals
Communicate findings to referring provider regarding elevated LDL/total cholesterol and nutrition barriers identified
redFlags: Untreated significantly elevated LDL (208.8 mg/dL) and total cholesterol (290 mg/dL) warranting medical follow-up
Chronic opioid use with unreported GI side effects potentially affecting nutritional intake

Patient reports 'saving'/rationing prescribed Percocet, raising a safety concern about medication use that should be flagged to the referring/prescribing provider (not confronted directly in this visit)
Caregiver burden with evidence of self-neglect (skipping her own meals) that may warrant social work or care-coordination referral
educationPoints: Explain in plain language how high cholesterol can build up over years without symptoms, and why the lab numbers matter even though she 'feels fine'
Clarify that frozen/fast food and gas-station snacks are often high in sodium and saturated fat, which can raise cholesterol over time
Suggest that small swaps (lower-sodium frozen meal, adding a piece of fruit, swapping one soda for water) are realistic first steps, not a full diet overhaul
Normalize that opioid medications commonly cause nausea and constipation, and that this is worth mentioning to her prescriber, as it may be affecting how much she eats
Reinforce that her caregiving role is demanding and that even very small nutrition changes can fit around her schedule without adding burden
Avoid framing education around weight loss; focus on energy, pain management, and lab numbers as motivators since those matter more to her

mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows multivitamin filled once over a year ago with no refills since (a12, d7)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported supplement adherence can diverge from objective refill records; explore discrepancies with curiosity rather than confrontation, as patients may round up or misremember infrequent habits.
